clusters.name: Hypothalamic appetite circuit
clusters.fact: In the arcuate nucleus, two opposed sets of neurons read the body's fuel signals. POMC neurons release α-MSH, which acts on melanocortin-4 receptors to curb eating and raise energy use; NPY/AgRP neurons drive eating and block those same receptors. The lateral hypothalamus is the feeding center whose loss abolishes hunger.

NPY/AgRP neurons.text: Arcuate neurons that release neuropeptide Y and agouti-related peptide, stimulating eating and blocking melanocortin-4 receptors.

POMC neurons.text: Arcuate neurons that make pro-opiomelanocortin and release α-MSH from it, reducing food intake and raising energy expenditure.

arcuate nucleus.text: A hypothalamic nucleus at the base of the brain, where circulating fuel signals reach the two opposed populations of appetite neurons.

lateral hypothalamus.text: Guyton's feeding center: stimulating it provokes eating, and destroying it abolishes the desire for food.

melanocortin-4 receptor.text: MC4R, the receptor on downstream hypothalamic neurons through which α-MSH curbs eating; AgRP blocks it.

clusters.name: Meal signals
clusters.fact: Signals from the gut regulate each meal. Ghrelin from the stomach rises before meals and stimulates hunger. Once food arrives, stretch of the stomach and hormones from the intestine, cholecystokinin, peptide YY, and GLP-1, produce satiety and bring the meal to an end.

GLP-1.text: Glucagon-like peptide-1, released by the intestine after a meal; it slows stomach emptying, curbs appetite, and boosts insulin release.

cholecystokinin.text: CCK, released by the upper small intestine in response to fat and protein; it signals satiety mainly through the vagus nerve.

termInfo.gastric distension: Stretch of the stomach wall as food fills it, sensed by stretch receptors and reported to the brainstem; it ends a meal regardless of the food's calories.

ghrelin.text: A hormone released mainly by the empty stomach; its level climbs before meals, falls after eating, and stimulates hunger through NPY/AgRP neurons.

peptide YY.text: A hormone released by the lower intestine after a meal, in proportion to the calories eaten, that reduces appetite.

clusters.name: Adiposity signals
clusters.fact: Fat tissue releases leptin in proportion to its mass, and insulin rises with body fat as well. Both reach the arcuate nucleus as long-term signals of stored energy. In most obesity, leptin is high but the brain responds to it poorly.

insulin.text: Besides its role in glucose control, insulin circulates in proportion to body fat and acts on the arcuate nucleus much as leptin does.

leptin.text: A hormone secreted by fat cells in proportion to fat mass; it stimulates POMC neurons and inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons.

termInfo.leptin resistance: A blunted brain response to leptin, so high levels fail to curb appetite; it is typical of common obesity, which extra leptin does not treat.

clusters.name: Energy expenditure
clusters.fact: Daily energy expenditure has three parts. The basal metabolic rate is the largest share in a sedentary adult; physical activity is the most variable; and digesting and storing each meal adds a smaller amount, the thermic effect of food.

basal metabolic rate.text: The energy used at complete rest to keep the body's cells working, about 60 to 70 percent of daily expenditure in a sedentary adult.

termInfo.physical activity: Energy spent on movement, from walking and fidgeting to exercise; the most variable part of daily expenditure.

thermic effect of food.text: The rise in energy use for several hours after a meal, as food is digested, absorbed, and stored; about 10 percent of daily expenditure. Guyton calls it the specific dynamic action of food.

bridges.fact: Leptin and insulin rise with fat mass and act on the arcuate nucleus, stimulating POMC neurons and inhibiting NPY/AgRP neurons, so eating falls as fat accumulates and rises as it is lost. The circuit's control of intake in turn sets fat mass, closing the loop.
bridges.info: Long-term feedback that holds body fat near a defended level; the idea goes back to Gordon Kennedy's lipostatic hypothesis of 1953.

bridges.fact: Sensory fibers of the vagus nerve carry stomach stretch and the satiety signal of cholecystokinin to the brainstem, which relays them to the hypothalamus to end the meal.

info.text: Sensory fibers in the vagus nerve that report on the state of the gut to the brainstem.

bridges.fact: As fat stores shrink during weight loss, leptin falls and energy expenditure drops by more than the loss of tissue can explain, slowing further loss and favoring regain.

info.text: A change in energy expenditure beyond what changes in body size predict; after weight loss it lowers expenditure.

bridges.fact: Body fat changes only when the energy taken in differs from the energy spent: the appetite circuit sets intake, the expenditure components set output, and the difference is stored as fat or drawn from it.

info.text: The relation between energy intake and energy expenditure; any lasting surplus or deficit changes the body's stored energy.

lenses.explanation: Hunger has a gut signal, ghrelin, and hypothalamic machinery that answers it. The other signals on the board end a meal or report how much fuel is stored.

reasons.NPY/AgRP neurons: Their peptides drive feeding and block the melanocortin-4 receptor.
reasons.ghrelin: Rising before meals, it activates NPY/AgRP neurons and brings on hunger.
reasons.lateral hypothalamus: Stimulating this feeding center provokes eating.

lenses.prompt: Which neurons does leptin activate to suppress eating?
lenses.explanation: Leptin works on both arcuate populations at once: it excites POMC neurons and inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons, pushing the balance toward eating less.

reasons.POMC neurons: Leptin excites them, and the α-MSH they release acts on melanocortin-4 receptors to curb eating.

lenses.prompt: Which gut hormones help bring a meal to an end?
lenses.explanation: Ghrelin rises before meals and works the other way. Stomach stretch also ends a meal, as a mechanical signal carried by nerves.

reasons.GLP-1: It slows stomach emptying and curbs appetite.
reasons.cholecystokinin: Fat and protein in the upper intestine release it, and it signals fullness through the vagus nerve.
reasons.peptide YY: The lower intestine releases it in proportion to the calories eaten.

lenses.prompt: Which hormone do weight-loss drugs such as semaglutide mimic?
lenses.explanation: A meal's own GLP-1 is cleared within minutes. A long-acting drug that activates its receptor around the clock keeps appetite low and stomach emptying slow.

reasons.GLP-1: Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors, but lasts far longer than the natural hormone.

lenses.prompt: Which nerve fibers carry stomach stretch to the brainstem?
lenses.explanation: The brainstem relays these signals to the hypothalamus. Cutting the vagal sensory fibers blunts much of cholecystokinin's satiety effect.

reasons.vagal afferents: Sensory fibers of the vagus nerve report stretch and cholecystokinin's signal from the gut.

lenses.prompt: Which pancreatic hormone also tells the hypothalamus how large the fat stores are?
lenses.explanation: Insulin carries two messages: after a meal it directs fuel into storage, and over the long term its level tracks how much fuel is already stored.

reasons.insulin: Its level rises with body fat, and it acts on the arcuate nucleus much as leptin does.

lenses.prompt: Which loop ties long-term food intake to the size of the fat stores?
lenses.explanation: Because the loop closes, body fat is defended in both directions: a meal skipped or a feast eaten is largely made up within days.

reasons.lipostatic feedback: Fat sets leptin and insulin, these signals set appetite, and appetite in turn sets fat.

lenses.prompt: Which condition explains why extra leptin fails to curb appetite in most obesity?
lenses.explanation: Leptin injections help only the rare people who cannot make leptin at all; in common obesity the signal is present but poorly heard.

reasons.leptin resistance: Leptin is already high in common obesity, but the brain responds to it weakly.

lenses.prompt: Loss of which receptor is the most common single-gene cause of severe obesity?
lenses.explanation: Farooqi and colleagues found these mutations in about 6 percent of people with severe obesity beginning in childhood.

reasons.melanocortin-4 receptor: Without working receptors, α-MSH cannot curb eating, so hunger persists despite ample fat stores.

lenses.prompt: Which part of daily energy expenditure rises after each meal?
lenses.explanation: It is the smallest of the three parts, about a tenth of daily expenditure; protein raises it more than fat or carbohydrate does.

reasons.thermic effect of food: Digesting, absorbing, and storing food raises energy use for several hours.

lenses.prompt: Which response slows weight loss as fat stores shrink?
lenses.explanation: The same intake that produced weight loss early in a diet produces less later, because the body is now spending less. This is a large part of why lost weight is often regained.

reasons.adaptive thermogenesis: Falling leptin lowers energy expenditure beyond what the smaller body explains.

lenses.prompt: Which principle says body fat changes only when intake and expenditure differ?
lenses.explanation: Every other concept on the board acts on one side of this relation or the other: the appetite circuit and meal signals on intake, the expenditure components on output, and the adiposity signals on both.

reasons.energy balance: Any lasting difference between energy taken in and energy spent is stored as fat or drawn from it.

entries.reason: See the other variable held near a set point by the hypothalamus, with brown fat and thyroid hormone as effectors.

learningIntroduction.title: How the body balances energy
learningIntroduction.summary: How the hypothalamus reads signals from the gut and from fat to set food intake, how the body spends energy, and why body fat is defended.

content.text:
Over a year an adult may eat close to a million kilocalories, yet body weight often changes by only a kilogram or two. Small mismatches between intake and use would add up quickly, so something must be matching them. The brain, gut, fat tissue, and pancreas share that work.

## The principle

The body obeys **energy balance**: stored energy, mostly fat, changes only when the energy taken in differs from the energy spent. Everything else in this lesson acts on one side of that relation or the other.

## The appetite circuit

The control center lies in the hypothalamus. In the **arcuate nucleus**, at the base of the brain, two opposed groups of neurons read the body's fuel signals. **POMC neurons** release α-MSH, which acts on the **melanocortin-4 receptor** to reduce eating and raise energy use. **NPY/AgRP neurons** do the reverse: they drive eating, and their AgRP blocks the melanocortin-4 receptor. The **lateral hypothalamus**, which Guyton calls the feeding center, provokes eating when stimulated; destroying it abolishes the desire for food.

## Signals from each meal

The gut regulates each meal. **Ghrelin**, released mainly by the empty stomach, rises before meals and stimulates hunger through the NPY/AgRP neurons. Once food arrives, signals of fullness take over. **Gastric distension**, the stretch of the stomach wall, and **cholecystokinin**, released by the upper intestine in response to fat and protein, are carried to the brainstem by **vagal afferents**, the sensory fibers of the vagus nerve. Further along, the intestine releases **peptide YY** in proportion to the calories eaten, and **GLP-1**, which slows stomach emptying and curbs appetite. Drugs such as semaglutide mimic GLP-1, but last far longer.

## Signals from stored fat

Meal signals end a meal but do not decide how much fat the body carries. That is the job of long-term signals. Fat cells release **leptin** in proportion to fat mass, and **insulin** also circulates in proportion to body fat. Both act on the arcuate nucleus, exciting POMC neurons and inhibiting NPY/AgRP neurons. The result is **lipostatic feedback**: as fat accumulates, eating falls, and as fat is lost, eating rises, while the circuit's control of eating in turn sets how much fat there is.

This loop explains why leptin seemed at first a promising treatment for obesity, and why it disappointed. People who cannot make leptin at all are severely obese and respond dramatically to it, but they are very rare. In common obesity, leptin is already high, and the brain responds to it weakly, a state called **leptin resistance**. Mutations in the melanocortin-4 receptor are the most common single-gene cause of severe obesity.

## Energy spent

Daily energy expenditure has three parts. The **basal metabolic rate**, the energy used at complete rest, is the largest share in a sedentary adult, about 60 to 70 percent. **Physical activity**, from fidgeting to exercise, is the most variable. The **thermic effect of food**, the energy used to digest, absorb, and store a meal, adds about 10 percent.

Expenditure does not stay fixed when weight changes. As fat stores shrink, leptin falls and expenditure drops by more than the smaller body can explain. This **adaptive thermogenesis** slows further weight loss and favors regain, and it is one reason body fat is defended so effectively against loss.
